paragraphs.source_en: The Tibetan people never blamed Tsangyang Gyatso for being romantic and unrestrained. As long as it was the feeling of a living Buddha, as long as it was something the living Buddha did, they accepted it; all the more so when such an extraordinary living Buddha should express emotions just like those of ordinary mortals. For that reason they cherished Tsangyang Gyatso even more. What ordinary people possess, Tsangyang Gyatso ought also to possess; since it had been taken from him, he naturally had the right to seek it and claim it. His genuine, bold, and rebellious nature stirred among Tibetans a special fondness for his love songs.

paragraphs.source_en: Tsangyang Gyatso wrote works such as The Love Songs of Tsangyang Gyatso. The Love Songs of Tsangyang Gyatso adopts the folk-song form of the xie style; it has musicality, insight, and spiritual quickness, often uses colloquial language, combines direct evocation with analogy, and possesses a strong folk-song character. The Love Songs are pure sounds of nature, a true portrayal of his life in love; one might also say they are the revelation of the heart of a religious rebel pursuing beauty and desire. He boldly pursued love and opposed the strangling of human nature.

paragraphs.source_en: In 1701, the fortieth year of Kangxi, Lhazang Khan secretly memorialized the Qing court, accusing Tsangyang Gyatso of improper conduct, with the intention of bringing down Sangye Gyatso, because the Sixth Dalai Lama had been appointed by Sangye Gyatso. In 1705, the forty-fourth year of Kangxi, Sangye Gyatso ordered someone to put poison in Lhazang Khan’s food, and from this a fierce war broke out. In 1705 Lhazang Khan marched on Lhasa. In 1706 Sangye Gyatso was captured and executed, and Tsangyang Gyatso, judged not to conform to religious discipline, was ordered to be sent to the capital. On the way under escort, the twenty-three-year-old living Buddha saw the light on Qinghai Lake and, as if hearing the call of a lover, began ceaselessly singing his own “la yi,” The Love Songs of Tsangyang Gyatso; Tsangyang Gyatso seemed all at once to have freed himself from the factional struggle represented by Sangye Gyatso and Lhazang Khan. paragraphs.source_en: In my view, this once again offers a mysterious interpretation of Tsangyang Gyatso’s being submerged in Qinghai Lake: are not swans and cranes both numinous beings of the lake, spirits of the water, and things in which lovesick sorrow may be lodged? Tsangyang Gyatso must have seen a white crane by Qinghai Lake, taken Qinghai Lake for “Litang,” and gone in search of the crane, turning into cloud and mist and dissolving into the boundless haze and waves of Qinghai Lake. Yet no one can truly understand. Even if one understood that he dissolved into Qinghai Lake, one still could not understand where he truly dissolved to. That is a kind of emptiness. Awakening to emptiness. It is a realm with no heaven, no earth, no you, and no me.

units.source_en: Tsangyang Gyatso must have seen a white crane by Qinghai Lake, taken Qinghai Lake for “Litang,” and gone in search of the crane, turning into cloud and mist and dissolving into the boundless haze and waves of Qinghai Lake.

paragraphs.source_en: No one knows what the living Buddha, dying in Qinghai Lake, actually heard or saw; still less does anyone know what his final hours were like. Yet there is no doubt that the Sixth Dalai Lama disappeared by the shores of Qinghai Lake. Sumba Khenpo’s History of Qinghai says: on the way to the capital, Tsangyang Gyatso died at Yangkanor Lake in the upper Qinghai region. The Biography of the Seventh Dalai Lama says: “…On the road, Tsangyang Gyatso received prostrations from tens of thousands of Han and Tibetan faithful.” Later he arrived at Gonggar and passed away there. His subordinates, remembering his kindness, prayed for him with tears in their eyes. Tsangyang Gyatso’s body was received and taken to Xining, where for several days believers made offerings and prayers. Instances of Tibetan Lamas records: “In the forty-sixth year, 1707, Tsangyang Gyatso reached the place of Gonggaluo in Qinghai and entered nirvana.” The official Chinese history Veritable Records of Shengzu says: “In the forty-fifth year of Kangxi, 1706, the Court of Colonial Affairs reported that lamas stationed in Xining had stated: the false Dalai Lama sent by Lhazang died of illness after reaching a place outside Xining Pass.”
